Thanks a lot for your explanation!

Anyways, I have another question about the individual heterozygosity values reported by the 2 functions filter.heterozygosity & report.heterozygosity.
In my data, the histogram for report.heterozygosity (method=ind) gives an histogram with values from 0.08 to 0.016 on the x-axis, but if I set as thresholds 0.10 and  0.15 (within the range of the reported values from the report.heterozygosity function) for the filter.heterozygosity function then i get the error "subscript out of bound" and the function tells me min individual heterozygosity is 3.5 and max is 9, so very different values.

I looked up the source code for the 2 functions and I  noticed that:
- in report.heterozygosity: individual heetrozygosity is calculated as % of heterozygous loci for each individual over all individuals dived by the number of loci (" c.hets[i] <- sum <https://rdrr.io/r/base/sum.html>(m[i,]==1,na.rm=TRUE <https://rdrr.io/r/base/logical.html>)/(nLoc(x)-c.na <http://c.na>[i]) ")
- in filter.heterozygosity: individual heterozygosity is calculated as % of heterozygous loci for each individual over all individuals BUT divided by the number of individuals (" c.hets[i] <- sum <https://rdrr.io/r/base/sum.html>(m[i,]==1,na.rm=TRUE <https://rdrr.io/r/base/logical.html>)/(nInd(x)-c.na <http://c.na>[i])" )

How come there is this difference in the calculation? Shouldn't the 2 function report the same thing or am I missing something?
Thanks a lot!
Gabriella

> You are right in your observation: DArT uses 0 for the reference homozygote, 1 for SNP homozygote and 2 for heterozygote. Conversely, dartR uses 0 for the reference homozygote, 1 for heterozygote and 2 for SNP homozygote.

> (a) It is the coding schema used by the package Adegenet, so it is difficult to move from this while maintaining access to all the Adegenet features;
> (b) It allows summing the codes to obtain the frequency of SNP's, which simplifies greatly the computational side of things.
>
> This information is documented in the manuals and vignettes of dartR.

> Please let us know whether this information solved your question.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luis,
I have a question on the HWE filter (gl.filter.hwe).
I am using the developer version (I will then test also the sex.linked filter and let you know if I have any problems with that in case - re: my other question in the forum).
I am a bit confused on which type of filtering this function applies.

I have read that you can filter genetic loci that depart from HWE in various ways (Pearman et al., 2021 - https://doi.org/10.1101/2021.06.15.448615): No loci removed based on HWE departures (‘No Filter’), loci removed if they exhibit departures in any sampling location (‘Out Any’), loci removed if they exhibit departures from HWE in all sampling locations (or a certain proportion of sampling locations) (‘Out All’, ‘Out Some’), or loci removed if they exhibit departures across sampling locations (‘Out Across’).

What kind of filtering is applied by the function gl.filter.hwe in the dev@dartR version?

I saw that you can decide whether to apply the filter to "each" population separately or to "all" populations considered as a whole large population.
Would the first option "each" be equivalent to the "OUT ANY" approach, removing ANY locus which deviates from HWE even just in a single population?

And what about the second option "all"? Would that remove only loci that are not in HWE in each of every populations taken singly (approach "OUT ALL")? Or would that instead remove loci that are deviating from HWE across the whole genomic dataset with all the populations merged together as if they were one (approach "OUT ACROSS")?

I am afraid that this last approach could have a big impact on the downstream analysis and reduce the genetic differentiation existing between populations..("differences in allele frequencies between populations leading to these loci being out of HWE when analysed at the total dataset level" - Pearman et al., 2021).

I think in my dataset the best approach would be to apply a HWE filter that removes loci which are out of HWE in ANY of the populations, so I would like to know if your filter option does that.

I would really appreciate some clarifications!
Thanks a lot as usual for your help!
Gabriella

messages.subject: Re: filtering on HWE departure
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabriella,

The dartR option "each", uses the slot @pop to define populations and tests the significance of HW departure within each population. The filter function (gl.filter.hwe) identifies those loci showing a significant departure at any population and then removes those loci from all the populations. So, this option corresponds to the option "OUT ANY" in the publication you mentioned.

The dartR option "all", merges all the individuals into one population and tests the significance of HW departure on this one population. The filter function removes all the loci departing from HWE. This option corresponds to the approach "OUT ACROSS".

Tests for HW proportions are only valid if there is no population substructure. So, yes, if your dataset contains discrete populations and you use the option "all", your results will be probably misleading.

Cheers,
Luis

Hi Gabriela,

You can use the code below to filter out loci departing from HW proportions in each population separately ("OUT ALL"). It would be important to consider how your downstream analyses would be affected by using a different set of loci in each population.

# separating populations and store them in a list
pop_list <- seppop(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>)
# filtering on HWE in every population
pop_list_hwe <- lapply(pop_list,gl.filter.hwe,method="Exact", multi_comp = T)

Regards,
Luis

Hi,

Isn’t a third option to identify loci that are “consistently” out if HWE across populations (you decide on how many pops is the threshold), and to remove those loci from the entire dataset? Otherwise you’re throwing out loci that are out of HWE in just a few pops by chance. I guess it depends on how you plan to use the data, and its probably wise whatever you do, to re-run analyses under a few HWE filtering scenarios to convince yourself (and reviewers) of the effectiveness (or not) of your approach.

Olly

Hello everyone,

Can anyone please suggest a solution to combine three datasets from the same Diversity Arrays service, where the files have been split due to size limitations? The three datasets each contain the same individuals and so have the same individual metadata, but different numbers of SNPs.

I believe this is a different issue than a previous conversation about rbind.genlight (26 Feb), as in the current case each genlight object contains the same individuals and the intent is not to reduce the number of SNPs (yet).

Extremely grateful for your help,
Thanks,
Caroline.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabriella,

To remove only those loci that deviate from Hardy-Weinberg proportions in all populations, you can use the code below.

library(dartR)

# separating populations and store them in a list
pop_list <- seppop(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>)

# reporting loci deviating from HW proportoins in every population
pop_list_hwe <- lapply(pop_list,gl.report.hwe,method="Exact", multi_comp = T)
# merging dataframes by row
loci_hwe_temp <- do.call(rbind,pop_list_hwe)
# finding loci that deviate in all populations
loci_hwe <-  loci_hwe_temp[duplicated(loci_hwe_temp$Locus),"Locus"]
# removing loci that deviate in all populations
pop_list_wo_hwe <- lapply(pop_list,gl.drop.loc,loc.list= loci_hwe)

Please let us know whether this worked for you.

Cheers,
Luis

messages.subject_clean: filter.sexlinked - error if change tolerance thresholds..
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabrielle,

Thanks for all your comments and suggestions. You are helping us make dartR better.

>
> 1. If I save the report results in an object, why the xxxy dataframe turns out to be "with 0 rows and 0 columns" ? Is it because the function tells me that "no sex linked markers consistent with male heterogamety have been identified" ? Does that mean there are no Y-linked loci?

Yes, it means there are no Y-linked or W-linked loci identified, depending on whether you have male or female heterogamety, respectively.

>
> 2. What do these functions (report/filter.sexlinked) really do? Do they identify loci that are sex-linked or instead alleles that are sex-linked?

If a locus is sex linked, then it is on the sex chromosomes in the non-recombining region.

If you have an allele at such a locus present on the X and not the Y (or the Z and not the W), then it will be present in full copy number in the XX and half copy number in the XY. So looking at read depth differences in the male (XY) and female (XX) individuals should be evident if there are sufficient data, but note that both the male XY and the female XX will have this allele. Unfortunately, the read depths of SNP data are not usually sufficiently high to support a definitive decision on their own.

If you have an allele at such a locus present on the Y but not the X then all male XY individuals will be heterozygous at that locus and all the female XX individuals will be homozygous at that locus. That is the signature our script looks for. We add in read depth information as supporting evidence.

If you are using SilicoDArT data, then you are working with presence-absence of sequence tags. That is a different kettle of fish and I am not sure we cover that in our script (at least not the bit I wrote).

If there is a mutation at the restriction-site or both restriction sites for the sequence on the X, then you will generate a homozygous NULL allele in female XX individuals (assuming there are not polymophisms in the X), and a positive call for the Y. So there you would be looking for all male XY animals with a positive call (could be homozygous depending on the thresholds used to make the calls) and missing calls for all XX female individuals. Read depth of the XY calls in comparison with the average across loci would be supporting evidence.

If thee is a mutation at the restriction-site or both restriction sites for the sequence on the Y, then you will generate a homozygous call for female XX individuals (assuming there are not polymophisms in the X), and a NULL or homozygous call in the male XY individuals depending on the thresholds used to make the calls. So these situations are not terribly informative without some serious sleuthing.

> I assume that
> - SEX-LINKED LOCI are loci that occur only in the X or in the Y chromosome:

We regard a locus to be sex linked if it is expressed in a fashion that differs between males and females. So it includes loci that occur only in the X or the Y chromosome AND loci that are present on both the X and Y chromosomes but which express a different product in each of the sexes.

> if the locus is Y-linked --> Females (XX) dont have that locus at all (so in dartR SNP dataset it would appear as "- -", correct?) and males are haploid (so in dart dataset "a -", where "a" is the Y-linked allele, and it would be removed by preliminary quality filtering)
> if the locus is X-linked --> Females can be both heterozygous for that locus (if they have both a Reference & a SNP allele) or homozygous (2 reference alleles/2 SNP alleles) or they can be only homozygous if the locus is monomorphic (as assumed by the functions?); males instead are again haploid for that locus (having only 1 allele for that locus coming from the female either the reference or the SNP allele, and no allele on the Y chromosome, so in dart it would appear as "a - " and it would be removed by preliminary quality filtering). Correct?

Correct, except I cannot say how a- will be called, as it depends on the thresholds in the filtering pipeline.

>
> - SEX-LINKED ALLELES are alleles that are occurring only on the Y or X chromosome for a locus that is shared by both the X and Y chromosome (not absent in either type of chromosome).
> So for example, specific SNPs that occurred only in the Y or only in the X chromosome but still within an autosomal-type/shared locus, but that specific SNP allele is not present in the other sex chromosome...is that correct? The "gl.report.sexlinked" function description says "Alleles unique to the Y or W chromosome and monomorphic on the X chromosomes will appear in the SNP dataset as genotypes that are heterozygotic in all individuals of the heterogametic sex and homozygous in all individuals of the homogametic sex. This function identifies loci with alleles that behave in this way, as putative sex specific SNP markers".
> So the function should be identifying only ALLELES (and not loci) that are sex-linked? But only those that are monomorphic n the X chromosome?

Yes, monomorphic in the XX individuals and heteromorphic in the XY individuals.

>
> If it does identify only alleles that are inherited as sex-linked but within shared loci (loci present on both X and Y chromosomes), then SNP alleles that are unique to the Y chromosome will be heterozygous in males (males have always only the SNP allele on the Y chromosome and the Ref allele on the X chromosome), and females will have only always 2 Ref alleles, so homozygous. So with the report/filter.sexlinked function, I would want to eliminate those loci, so I would use t.het for this correct, with t.het=0.5 allows 5% of the heterogametic sex to be homozygous and still be regarded as Y-linked, correct? And then t.hom to allow only a small percentage of Females (homogametic sex) to be heterozygous
>
> However, for SNP alleles that are X-linked though, if the locus is monomorphic in Females, so females have only the SNP allele (correct?) then Females would be always homozygous (2 SNP alleles) & Males would be always heterozygous (1 SNP allele from X-Chr and 1 Ref allele for Y-chr), right? So the thresholds work in the same way for both X- or Y- linked alleles?

Hmmm. The problem is that the user might want to make a distinction between sex-specific alleles and sex-linked alleles. Sex specific alleles are on the sex chromosomes in the non-recombining region; sex linked loci are (in addition) loci that reside close to the non-recombining region, that is, in the pseudoautosomal region, and so linked to some degree. If interested in removing all loci with sex linked alleles, you might want to adjust t.het and t.hom. There is also the issue of mis-calls or maybe the odd ring-in individual. Again, a less than absolute threshold might be appropriate.

>
> If I try to change t-het & t.hom in different combinations, i.e.-  t.het=0.05 t.hom=0.05  --> the results tell "
> Sex linked loci consistent with female heterogamety (ZZ/ZW)
> Threshold proportion for homozygotes in the heterozygotic sex (ZW) is 0.05
> Threshold proportion for heterozygotes in the homozygotic sex (ZZ) is 0.05"
> and below there are 7 sex-linked loci listed, which I assume are the sex-linked loci that are removed and I think they are all represented by those points in the plot lying on the x-axis & with high female heterozygosity (close to 1), so they have high female heterozygosity & are totally homozygous in males (because they lay on the x-axis), but from the reasoning above (sex-linked alleles), there cannot be any loci which are homozygous in males and considered sex-linked...
> so what is the function really doing? I am quite confused? are these sex linked loci and if so X or Y linked? And also, if they are what do they represent? And can you differentiate between the X-linked and the Y-linked loci?

In this case, the script has identified that you have a female heterogametic species, that is with ZZ males and ZW females. It cannot be interpreted in the context of an XX/XY system.

>
> 3. Also what do the threshold really mean? I read the definition but I'm still very confused.
> So, by the definition in the R function description:
> - the threshold "t.het" is supposed to allow a certain percentage (0.05 =5%) of the heterogametic sex (so the males) to be homozygote for the locus & still consider the locus as sex-linked ("t.het=0.05 means that 5% of the heterogametic sex can be homozygous and still be regarded as consistent with a sex specific marker") So it allows a certain range of "error" (5% in this case) in the detection of loci which are X?-linked and therefore should be heterozygous in 100% of the males.

Yes, for a male heterogametic system. For a female heterogametic system, swap male for female -- "Z-linked and therefore should be heterozygous in 100% of the females".

>
> However, when I run the gl.report.sexlinked function with t.het=0.20 & t.hom=0.05, in the results I read:
> "Threshold proportion for heterozygotes in the homozygotic sex (ZZ) is 0.2"
>
> "Threshold proportion for homozygotes in the heterozygotic sex (ZW) is 0.05"
>
> the two definitions of t.het (and of t.hom) in the results seem contrasting with that from the function manual....this is one of the confusing things..

That looks like a bug. I will attend to it.

>
> Then, by modifying alternatively one or the other threshold, i realized that changing "t.het" changes the length of the yellow threshold area on the plot (horizontal length on the x-axis, vertical length on the y-axis). So increasing t.het I remove more loci which are totally homozygous in males but with levels of heterozygosity decreasing from 100% to the value of the threshold (t.het=0.20 means it removes loci homozygous for males and with female heterozygosity between 80-100%). While, changing the value of "t.hom", changes the width of the yellow threshold area (area of filtered loci) (the height of the area in the vertical direction on the x -axis, and the width of the yellow area in the horizontal direction on the y-axis). So by increasing t.hom, I remove more loci which have high female heterozygosity and decreasing male homozygosity (so a threshold of t.hom =0.20 filters out loci with males homozygosity between 80-100%). Is this interpretation correct? Anyways, I still cannot understand how is this approach removing sex-linked loci...
>
> I would really appreciate some clarifications as I have been trying to understand this for a while now and I keep getting confused...

The graphic was added by someone else. I will need to confer with them and get back to you.

>
> Thanks a lot
>
> Gabriella
> > > >

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] output structure file
messages.body_plain:
Hi Evgenii,

If you are using SNP' data, it doesn't matter if you use any of the two formats. According to Structure manual:
"Unless you plan to use the linkage model, the order of the alleles for a single individual does not matter"

It doesn't matter what character you use for missing data because you can set this value, as described in the Structure manual:
"the missing data value is set along with the other parameters describing the characteristics of the data set"

Cheers,
Luis

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] output structure file
messages.body_plain:
Hi Evgenii,

Most of the SNPs are bi-allelic (0.3% of SNPs have more than two alleles in humans). However, dartR, which uses a genlight object to store genetic data, can deal only with bi-allelic SNPs. SNPs with more than two alleles are removed either by DArT, when reading your dataset by using functions such as gl.read.vcf or when the data is converted into a genlight object. However, it is always important to double-check your data. In your example, there are some loci that have more than three alleles, which is not possible for the reasons explained above. So, it doesn't matter whether you use any of the two formats, the only important thing is that each of the two alleles in each locus is coded by a unique integer, as described in Structure manual.

To convince yourself, you can try to run Structure using both approaches, in a subset of your dataset, and using the same seed number. You can find how to set this seed number in Structure manual.

Cheers,
Luis
